body_markdown:
It would be easy to assume that the Baja Package worn by this 1989 S-10, with its light bar, chunky BFGoodrich all-terrains, and graphics, was simply an aesthetic flourish. And that’s true: the Baja Package didn’t offer a hard-core kit like trick shocks or a functional roll bar. As the[brochure](https://xr793.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/1989-Chevrolet-S10.pdf) warns, “Note: The light support on this truck is not


a roll bar. The support won’t protect you in an accident.” But the package wasn’t simply an effort to keep up with the times. It was a nod to Chevrolet’s partnership with off-road-racing veterans Team MacPherson at the[Baja 1000](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/how-to-race-in-the-baja-1000-on-the-cheap/) .


The rad street presence and the nod to history worked in favor of this particular example; even with 76,000 miles and a history involving some bumps and bruises, this 76,000-mile example drew enthusiastic bidding, selling recently on Bring a Trailer for[$23,625](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1989-chevrolet-s-10-19/) with fees.


The 1982 S-10 was part of Detroit’s answer to[compact trucks](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-story-of-the-small-truck-past-present-and-future/) from Datsun and Toyota, and its combination of maneuverability, simplicity, and ladder-frame durability has aged well. **** New for 1989, the Baja option was a “rugged off-road appearance package” that included specific paint and graphics, a tubular rear bumper, a light bar with off-road lamps, and black/chrome accents on the head- and taillight bezels and grille. It was available on any 4×4 S-10—as long as you ordered the top-level trim (Tahoe, not to be confused with the subsequent SUV, which arrived in ’95), the 1500-pound payload package, underbody “shield package,” and the 2.8-liter V-6. So picky, Chevy!

Whoever ordered our featured truck didn’t stop there. This Maxi Cab S-10 was also ordered with deep tint, manual sunroof, reclining seat backs, front color-keyed floor mats, the optional four-speed automatic transmission, front A/C, aluminum wheels, electronic speed control, a driver convenience package which brought a tilting steering wheel and intermittent wipers, a 3.42:1 rear-axle ratio, engine-block heater, and the 4.3-liter V-6. Essentially a 5.7 minus two cylinders, the 4.3 was standard in the full-size Chevy trucks, and the top-spec engine in the S-10. It made 160 hp at 4000 rpm and 230 lb-ft of torque at 2800 rpm.


In total, this truck carries $4872 in options, bringing the total to $16,957 plus a $400 destination fee (what innocent days)—$17,357.00, or about $47,000 today. Cheaper than a mid-size Colorado ZR2 by about $6K!


eBay / GallimoresGoods


Now, for a quick excursion into history. In 1982, Joe MacPherson and Jerry McDonald ran a stock Chevy S-10 pickup in the famously grueling Baja 1000 in Mexico. (To be fair, “stock” included the optional V-6, four-wheel drive, and the optional off-road chassis package.) Like other endurance races, attrition is high, and simply finishing is a victory. However, neither MacPherson nor McDonald were new to the race or to the sport: Ten years before, the duo had formed Team MacPherson Motorsports. MacPherson was a California Chevy dealer, and McDonald a talented fabricator and designer. The first vehicle they took to Baja? A Chevy Blazer. In short, it was entirely natural that they took an S-10 to Baja the year the little pickup came out. The little S-10 took 37 hours to finish the race, but it finished. (Race winner Mickey Thompson in his specially built Volkswagen[did it in 19 hours](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jKmWeJD9t64) .)

The BaT truck comes with “Baja” seat covers.


MacPherson proved hugely successful at Baja, winning 10 class championships and 83 wins over 28 years. For 16 of those years, MacPherson was a factory partner with GM, helping to test and develop electronic four-wheel drive on its race trucks before the tech made production. Thanks to the success of Team MacPherson, both Joe and Jerry were inducted into the Off-Road Motorsports Hall of Fame.


With that background, and considering how hard Chevrolet leaned into the Baja-tackling ability of the S-10 in this 1986 ad, it’s almost surprising that we didn’t get a Baja appearance package until seven years *after* the truck first tackled the famous race.


Even so, this ’89 Baja-package S-10 is attention-grabbing today, whether or not you know the story behind those red-and-black graphics. We don’t include the 1982–93 S-10 in our price guide, but our quote data reveals that Gen X and younger enthusiasts are disproportionately interested in the model. This truck’s $23,625 result is one of the higher figures for an S-10 of this generation in the last five years on Bring a Trailer—especially considering that this truck had an unfortunate run-in with a curb in 1996 that required a new fender and wheel well housing, according to the seller. “Fortunately it happened when the truck was still pretty new, so insurance paid for the full OEM parts and repairs,” they add in the comments.


Even so, this Chevy kept on trucking in the 30 years since, and it appears to have a lot of life left. Spending $24K on an old S-10 may seem surprising, but it’s a testament to the appeal of off-road adventure and ’80s nostalgia—and this truck has both in spades, plus a cool origin story. It just needs a set of white-letter BFGoodrichs, and it’s good to go.
